functional-alloys-001.question: Compared with the martensitic transformation of quenched carbon steel, which is a correct feature of the thermoelastic martensitic transformation that occurs in shape memory alloys such as Ti-Ni?
choices: Because the transformation proceeds by diffusion of carbon or other atoms, the same amount of martensite forms at the same temperature whether cooling is slow or fast
The thermal hysteresis is small, martensite plates grow and shrink as the temperature goes down and up, and on heating the alloy returns reversibly to the original parent phase
Because martensite has a much larger volume than the parent phase, many dislocations are introduced at every transformation, making the alloy harder and stronger each time
functional-alloys-001.explanation: In a thermoelastic transformation, the interface between the parent phase and martensite moves easily while staying coherent, and the shape change accompanying the transformation is accommodated mainly elastically. The transformation therefore proceeds reversibly with temperature, the martensite plates growing as the temperature falls and shrinking as it rises, and the thermal hysteresis is small, a few tens of kelvin in Ti-Ni. In quenched steel the shape change is accommodated by plastic deformation, the interfaces become immobile, and on heating carbon precipitation (tempering) occurs first, so the steel never returns directly to the original austenite. Both kinds of martensitic transformation are diffusionless, so the description that the transformation proceeds by diffusion is wrong. A large volume change that keeps introducing dislocations destroys reversibility and is the opposite of a thermoelastic feature.

functional-alloys-002.question: A Ti-Ni alloy wire has transformation temperatures Mf = 20 °C, Ms = 35 °C, As = 45 °C and Af = 60 °C, and the highest temperature at which stress-induced martensite can form, Md (above which the wire deforms plastically by slip before transforming), is about 150 °C. When the wire was bent by a few percent at some temperature and the load removed, it stayed bent; when it was then heated to 70 °C, it became straight again. Which was the bending temperature?
functional-alloys-002.explanation: At 10 °C, below Mf, the whole wire is martensite. Bending deforms it by aligning the variants, and it stays bent after the load is removed. When it is heated to 70 °C, above Af (60 °C), all the martensite returns to the parent phase and the original straight shape is restored. This is the shape memory effect. At 80 °C, above Af and below Md, bending produces stress-induced martensite, but it reverts to the parent phase as soon as the load is removed and the wire straightens (superelasticity), so it does not stay bent. At 250 °C, above Md, the wire deforms by dislocation slip in the parent phase, so it stays bent but does not recover on heating. The shape memory effect appears when the alloy is deformed in the martensitic state and then heated above Af.

functional-alloys-003.question: Even when a shape memory alloy is cooled from the parent phase into martensite, its external shape hardly changes. Which correctly explains how it can be deformed in that state and then recover its original shape on heating?
choices: Dislocations accumulate at high density in the martensite formed on cooling, and on heating these dislocations disappear, so the deformation disappears with them
Deformation melts part of the martensite into liquid, and on heating the liquid resolidifies in its original position, reproducing the original shape
Many variants are arranged so that their shape changes cancel, and deformation aligns them; on heating they return to one definite parent orientation
functional-alloys-003.explanation: When the parent phase transforms on cooling, several kinds of variants with different habit planes form from one parent crystal. Each variant carries a shear shape change in a definite direction, but they combine and arrange themselves so that these cancel one another (self-accommodation), and the overall shape hardly changes. When force is applied in this state, twin boundaries and variant boundaries move, the variants matching the direction of the force grow, and a few percent of deformation proceeds without dislocation slip. On heating, every variant can return only to one definite orientation of the ordered parent lattice, so the original shape revives together with the original crystal. Saying that the shape recovers because dislocations disappear confuses this with recovery; deformation by dislocation slip is not reversed by heating. No liquid forms in this temperature range.

functional-alloys-004.question: Which correctly describes the difference between the one-way and two-way shape memory effects in shape memory alloys?
choices: One-way only returns to the memorized shape on heating; two-way also takes another shape on cooling, but needs training
One-way recovers shape on heating and two-way on removing the load, and the two-way shape memory effect refers to the same phenomenon as superelasticity
One-way can be used only once and two-way can be repeated any number of times, and both are present as soon as the alloy is melted, without training
functional-alloys-004.explanation: The ordinary shape memory effect is one-way: a part deformed in the martensitic state returns to its memorized shape on heating, but on cooling from there the variants again arrange themselves so that they cancel, and the shape does not change. If it is deformed again, the cycle can be repeated any number of times. The two-way shape memory effect is the property of changing spontaneously to a high-temperature shape on heating and to a low-temperature shape on cooling. It is obtained by training, repeated deformation in martensite and heating, or by aging under constraint, which creates internal stress fields from dislocations or precipitates so that particular variants form preferentially on cooling. The recovered strain is smaller than one-way and tends to decrease with cycling, so one-way elements combined with a bias spring are often used instead. Recovery on removing the load is superelasticity, a phenomenon different from the two-way shape memory effect.

functional-alloys-005.question: In a Ti-Ni alloy with about 50.8 at% Ni, assume that the transformation temperatures fall by about 10 K for every 0.1 at% increase in Ni. Near this composition, a change of 0.1 in at% Ni also changes the mass% by almost 0.1. To keep Af within ±5 K of its target, within about how many grams must the error in the mass of Ni be held when melting 1 kg of the alloy?
choices: About 5 g
About 0.5 g
About 0.05 g
functional-alloys-005.explanation: Dividing the ±5 K window by the sensitivity of 10 K per 0.1 at% gives ±0.05 at% Ni, which near this composition is almost ±0.05 mass%. For 1 kg of alloy, 1000 g × 0.0005 = 0.5 g, so the error in the mass of Ni must be held within about 0.5 g. About 5 g is the value obtained by misreading 0.05% as 0.005 (0.5%), one order of magnitude too large, and about 0.05 g errs by one order of magnitude in the other direction. On the Ni-rich side of Ti-Ni, a slight difference in composition changes the transformation temperatures greatly, so even the evaporation of Ni during melting and the loss of Ti tied up with oxygen and carbon are controlled, and finally the transformation temperatures of the melted material are measured to confirm them. Heat treatment is also used to fine-tune the transformation temperatures.

functional-alloys-006.question: When a Ni-rich Ti-Ni alloy is solution-treated and then aged at 400–500 °C, Ti₃Ni₄ (also written Ni₄Ti₃) precipitates and the transformation temperatures rise. What is the main reason?
choices: The precipitates stop dislocation motion and strengthen the matrix, and the stronger the matrix, the smaller the driving force needed for transformation, so the transformation temperatures rise
The matrix lattice is strained around the precipitates, so the melting point of the matrix falls by the amount of strain, and the transformation temperatures rise along with it
Ni-rich precipitates lower the Ni content of the remaining matrix, and the Ni-sensitive transformation temperatures rise
functional-alloys-006.explanation: Ti₃Ni₄ is a compound with a higher proportion of Ni than the Ti-Ni matrix. When it precipitates, the corresponding Ni leaves the matrix, so the Ni content of the matrix falls. On the Ni-rich side, the less Ni, the higher the transformation temperatures, so aging raises them. Changing the aging temperature and time changes the amount of precipitation, so this is used to adjust the transformation temperatures to the desired values after melting, and it is also known to make an intermediate phase, the R phase, appear more readily. The precipitates strengthen the matrix and improve the stability of superelasticity under cycling, but a stronger matrix does not mean that a smaller driving force for transformation suffices. A chain in which lattice strain lowers the melting point and raises the transformation temperatures also does not explain the change.

functional-alloys-007.question: The temperature dependence of the stress σ needed for stress-induced martensitic transformation is given by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation dσ/dT = ρ·|ΔH|/(T·ε), where ρ is the density, ΔH the latent heat of transformation per unit mass, ε the transformation strain in the tensile direction and T the absolute temperature. With ρ = 6.45 g/cm³, |ΔH| = 15 J/g, ε = 0.050 and T = 300 K, which is closest to dσ/dT?
choices: About 6.5 MPa/K
About 0.32 MPa/K
About 72 MPa/K
functional-alloys-007.explanation: The latent heat per unit volume is ρ|ΔH| = 6.45 g/cm³ × 15 J/g ≈ 96.8 J/cm³ = 9.68×10⁷ J/m³. Dividing by T·ε = 300 × 0.050 = 15 K gives dσ/dT ≈ 6.45×10⁶ Pa/K ≈ 6.5 MPa/K; J/m³ is the same unit as Pa. About 0.32 MPa/K is the value obtained by forgetting to divide by the transformation strain, and about 72 MPa/K by using the temperature as 27 °C instead of the absolute temperature. For superelasticity in Ti-Ni, slopes of about 6–7 MPa/K are often reported from measurements as well, so a 10 K rise in temperature raises the plateau stress by more than 60 MPa. This is why the force of a medical device used at body temperature differs greatly from the value measured at room temperature.

functional-alloys-008.question: In a Ti-Ni alloy, the stress at which stress-induced martensitic transformation begins is given by σ = 6.5 MPa/K × (T − Ms), with Ms = −20 °C. If the stress at which the parent phase yields by slip is 500 MPa independent of temperature, which is closest to the upper temperature limit for superelasticity (the temperature at which slip begins to occur before transformation)?
choices: About 77 °C
About 57 °C
About 37 °C
functional-alloys-008.explanation: Finding the temperature at which the stress needed for transformation equals the slip stress of 500 MPa gives T − Ms = 500/6.5 ≈ 77 K, so T ≈ −20 + 77 = 57 °C. Above this temperature the parent phase yields by slip before transformation occurs, leaving permanent strain that does not recover on unloading, so superelasticity must be used below this temperature (near Md). About 77 °C is the value obtained by taking 500/6.5 directly as the temperature without subtracting Ms, and about 37 °C by subtracting Ms of −20 °C twice. In practice, superelasticity is used in a temperature range above Af and well below this limit. Raising the slip stress of the parent phase by precipitates or working extends this range toward higher temperatures.

functional-alloys-009.question: Which is the main mechanism by which Mn-Cu damping alloys absorb vibration energy and convert it into heat?
choices: Ferromagnetic domain boundaries (domain walls) move irreversibly under stress, and energy is lost through magnetic hysteresis
Slip and friction occur at the interfaces between flake graphite dispersed in the matrix and the matrix, and energy is lost there
Fine twin boundaries formed by a transformation move back and forth under stress, and energy is lost through the resistance to their motion
functional-alloys-009.explanation: In Mn-Cu alloys rich in Mn, aging or cooling changes the FCC parent phase into a tetragonal structure, forming many fine twins inside. When vibrating stress is applied, the twin boundaries move back and forth according to the direction of the stress, and vibration energy is converted into heat in proportion to the resistance to that motion. Damping is therefore large in the temperature range where twins exist, and becomes small when the twins disappear above the transformation temperature. Irreversible domain-wall motion is the mechanism of the ferromagnetic type, such as Fe-Cr alloys, and the interfaces between flake graphite and the matrix that of the composite type in flake graphite cast iron; these are different kinds of damping materials. There is also a dislocation type, as in Mg, in which energy is lost as dislocations break away from impurities and move, and the dependence on temperature, amplitude and magnetic field differs by mechanism.

functional-alloys-010.question: When a cantilever plate was set vibrating freely, its amplitude fell to half its initial value in 10 cycles. Assuming the amplitude falls by the same ratio each cycle, which is closest to the fraction of vibration energy lost per cycle (the specific damping capacity) obtained from the logarithmic decrement δ = ln(Aₙ/Aₙ₊₁)? Assume the vibration energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
choices: About 13%
About 6.7%
About 5.0%
functional-alloys-010.explanation: Because the amplitude halves in 10 cycles, δ = ln 2/10 ≈ 0.0693. The amplitude ratio per cycle is Aₙ₊₁/Aₙ = e^(−δ) ≈ 0.933, and since energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude, the energy remaining after one cycle is e^(−2δ) ≈ 0.871. The fraction lost is 1 − 0.871 ≈ 0.13, about 13%, which for small δ can be approximated by 2δ ≈ 14%. About 6.7% mistakes the fractional loss of amplitude, 1 − e^(−δ), for the fraction of energy, and about 5.0% simply divides the fall in amplitude (50%) by the number of cycles. The specific damping capacity is expressed as ΔW/W in this way; for ordinary steel it is below 1%, whereas some damping alloys exceed 10%.

functional-alloys-011.question: Which is a correct property of ferromagnetic-type damping alloys such as Fe-Cr alloys?
choices: The more magnetic domains, the smaller the damping, so applying a strong field to divide the domains finely makes the damping even larger
In a field strong enough to saturate the magnetization, domain walls disappear, so the walls that move under stress are lost and the damping drops greatly
Damping comes from grain-boundary sliding, so it is unaffected by magnetic fields and becomes larger at higher temperatures as the grain boundaries move
functional-alloys-011.explanation: In ferromagnetic damping alloys, vibrating stress moves domain walls (especially 90° walls) irreversibly, producing a magnetic hysteresis in the stress–strain relation, and energy is lost in proportion to its area. When a strong field saturates the magnetization, the whole alloy becomes like a single domain and the domain walls disappear, so the walls that move under stress are lost and the damping drops greatly. These alloys therefore cannot be used near strong magnets. Also, large internal stresses from cold working and the like make domain walls hard to move, so the alloys are annealed before use. Saying that a field divides the domains finely is the opposite of what happens; a field aligns the domains with itself and reduces their number. Grain-boundary sliding is a different damping mechanism that occurs at high temperature and is not the main mechanism of the ferromagnetic type.

functional-alloys-012.question: The PCT curve (pressure–composition–temperature isotherm) of a hydrogen storage alloy shows a flat region (a plateau) where the hydrogen pressure stays nearly constant even as the amount of hydrogen increases. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Hydrogen is only adsorbed on the metal surface without entering the interior, and the pressure does not change until the surface is covered with hydrogen
Taking in hydrogen raises the temperature of the alloy, and the temperature rise exactly cancels the rise in pressure, so the curve appears flat
Over the range where a hydrogen-poor solid-solution phase and a hydride phase coexist, the phase rule fixes a single equilibrium pressure at a given temperature
functional-alloys-012.explanation: While there is little hydrogen, it dissolves in the interstices of the metal lattice to form the α phase, and the amount of hydrogen increases with pressure. Beyond a certain amount, the hydride β phase begins to form, and three phases coexist: α, β and hydrogen gas. With two components, metal and hydrogen, the phase rule gives F = C − P + 2 = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1, so once the temperature is fixed the equilibrium pressure is fixed too. The pressure therefore stays nearly constant while the α phase changes into β, giving the plateau. Once everything is β, the amount of hydrogen again increases a little with pressure. Adsorption on the surface alone cannot store amounts exceeding 1% of the mass of the alloy. A PCT curve is an isotherm measured at constant temperature, so the explanation that a temperature rise cancels the pressure does not hold either.

functional-alloys-013.question: Assume that the plateau pressure P of a hydrogen storage alloy follows the van 't Hoff equation ln P = ΔH/(RT) − ΔS/R. If the enthalpy of hydride formation is ΔH = −30 kJ/mol H₂ and the plateau pressure at 25 °C is 0.20 MPa, which is closest to the plateau pressure at 80 °C? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 1.3 MPa
About 0.24 MPa
About 0.030 MPa
functional-alloys-013.explanation: The difference of the equation at the two temperatures is ln(P₂/P₁) = (ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁), and with T₁ = 298.15 K and T₂ = 353.15 K, ln(P₂/P₁) = (−30000/8.314) × (−5.22×10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.88 and P₂/P₁ ≈ 6.6. Therefore P₂ ≈ 0.20 × 6.6 ≈ 1.3 MPa. Hydride formation is exothermic, so raising the temperature raises the plateau pressure, and heating releases hydrogen at a high pressure. About 0.24 MPa is the value obtained by treating the gas pressure as proportional to absolute temperature, 0.20 × 353/298, and about 0.030 MPa by reversing the sign of ΔH so that the pressure falls. The ΔH of LaNi₅ hydride is reported to be about −30 kJ/mol H₂.

functional-alloys-014.question: LaNi₅ absorbs hydrogen to become LaNi₅H₆. Which is closest to the mass of hydrogen as a percentage of the mass of the hydride (mass%)? Use atomic weights La 138.91, Ni 58.69 and H 1.008.
choices: About 2.7%
About 1.4%
About 7.7%
functional-alloys-014.explanation: The formula weight of LaNi₅ is 138.91 + 5 × 58.69 = 432.36, and the mass of six hydrogen atoms is 6 × 1.008 = 6.05, so 6.05/(432.36 + 6.05) ≈ 0.0138, about 1.4%. About 2.7% counts H₆ as six hydrogen molecules (12 H atoms), and about 7.7% corresponds to the hydrogen fraction of MgH₂, 2.016/(24.31 + 2.016). LaNi₅ can store an amount per volume comparable to liquid hydrogen, but because it consists of heavy elements the amount per mass is small, making it suited to stationary storage and to the negative electrodes of nickel–metal hydride batteries. Mg stores much more per mass, but its hydride is too stable, and releasing hydrogen at about 1 atm requires a high temperature of about 300 °C.

functional-alloys-015.question: Single crystals of Ni₂MnGa-based magnetic shape memory alloys produce large strains of a few percent simply when a magnetic field is applied in the martensitic state. Which is the correct mechanism?
choices: The field transforms the parent phase into martensite, and the volume change on transformation appears directly as a strain of a few percent
When the magnetization direction rotates in the field, the magnetostriction from slight changes in interatomic distance is more than 100 times larger than in other alloys
The magnetocrystalline anisotropy is large, so twin boundaries move to align the easy axis with the field
functional-alloys-015.explanation: Tetragonal martensite in Ni₂MnGa-based alloys has a large magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and the magnetization strongly prefers a particular crystal axis. When a field is applied, variants whose axis lies close to the field direction have lower energy, so mobile twin boundaries move and those variants grow. The difference in the lengths of the tetragonal axes becomes a change of shape directly, and strains of about 6% have been obtained in single crystals. The difference from the ordinary shape memory effect is that the field does not transform the parent phase into martensite but exchanges the orientations of variants while the material stays martensitic. Magnetostriction is the lattice strain accompanying rotation of the magnetization; it is of the order of 10⁻⁵ in Fe and Ni and only about 10⁻³ even in giant-magnetostriction alloys, far short of a few percent.

functional-alloys-016.question: Which statement correctly describes Fe-Mn-Si shape memory alloys?
choices: Stress forms HCP ε martensite in the FCC parent, and heating reverts it to restore the shape; they are cheap but recover a few percent strain or less, and are used for pipe couplings
Stress forms BCC α′ martensite in the FCC parent phase, and the temperature hysteresis is only a few kelvin, so they suit sensors and actuators that respond sensitively to temperature
Like Ti-Ni, the B2 parent phase transforms thermoelastically to B19′ martensite, so they show several percent of superelasticity at room temperature and are used for medical guidewires
functional-alloys-016.explanation: In Fe-Mn-Si alloys, deforming the FCC austenite makes Shockley partial dislocations move in a regular way, producing HCP ε martensite with a changed stacking sequence. On heating the partials move back, the parent phase is restored and the shape recovers. Because they are iron-based, inexpensive and easy to work, they are used for fastening parts such as pipe couplings, but the recoverable strain is a few percent or less, the transformation is not thermoelastic and the temperature hysteresis is large. If BCC α′ martensite forms, the shape is not recovered on heating, so Mn is added to suppress it and Si to assist the transformation to ε and the shape recovery. Thermoelastic B2-to-B19′ transformation and superelasticity are characteristic of Ti-Ni.

functional-alloys-017.question: Copper-based shape memory alloys such as Cu-Al-Ni and Cu-Zn-Al are cheaper than Ti-Ni, but as polycrystals they crack easily in repeated use. What is the main reason?
choices: The transformation strain is as small as about 0.1%, so large stresses are needed to obtain a shape memory effect and the parent phase fatigues
Because they contain much copper their electrical resistance is very high, so resistive heating overheats them to the point of local melting and they crack at grain boundaries
The parent phase has large elastic anisotropy and coarse grains, so transformation strain differs greatly between grains and stress concentrates at boundaries, causing cracking
functional-alloys-017.explanation: The parent phase of copper-based shape memory alloys is an ordered phase based on body-centered cubic, called the β phase; its elastic modulus varies strongly with direction (large elastic anisotropy) and its grains tend to be coarse. The transformation strain is set by the crystal orientation, so neighboring grains with different orientations deform incompatibly, large stresses concentrate at the grain boundaries and intergranular cracking occurs. Remedies include refining the grains with additions such as B, Ti or Zr, or using single crystals or strongly oriented structures. The transformation strain is several percent, not about 0.1%. Copper-based alloys actually have a low electrical resistance, and the difficulty of resistive heating is cited as a drawback.

functional-alloys-018.question: In Ti-Ni alloys heat-treated at a suitable temperature after cold working, the B2 parent phase may transform on cooling to a rhombohedral R phase before forming B19′ martensite. Which statement correctly describes the R-phase transformation?
choices: Its temperature hysteresis is small, a few kelvin or less, and its transformation strain is about 1% or less, so it suits temperature-responsive elements operating repeatedly
Its temperature hysteresis is large, several tens of kelvin, and its transformation strain is large, about 8%, so it suits pipe couplings that are tightened strongly just once
The R phase refers to the Ti₃Ni₄ precipitates themselves; it does not transform but hardens the parent phase and removes the shape memory effect
functional-alloys-018.explanation: In the R-phase transformation, the cubic lattice of the B2 parent phase is slightly elongated along a body diagonal to become rhombohedral. Because the lattice change is small, the transformation strain is about 1% or less and the temperature hysteresis is small, only a few kelvin. The small strain makes it resistant to degradation on cycling, and it operates precisely over a narrow temperature range, so it is used in elements such as thermally actuated valves. Dislocation structures formed by heat treatment after cold working, and Ti₃Ni₄ precipitates formed by aging Ni-rich alloys, hinder the transformation to B19′, so the R phase tends to appear first. A hysteresis of several tens of kelvin and large strains are characteristics of the transformation to B19′. The R phase is not a precipitate but a phase formed by transformation of the parent phase.

functional-alloys-019.question: A Ti-Ni wire 0.50 mm in diameter and 100 mm long carries a hanging weight and is heated so that it contracts by the shape memory effect. If the stress in the wire is constant at 200 MPa and the contraction strain is 4.0%, which is closest to the work done in lifting the weight? Neglect changes in cross-sectional area.
choices: About 0.63 J
About 0.079 J
About 0.16 J
functional-alloys-019.explanation: The cross-sectional area is π × (0.25×10⁻³)² ≈ 1.96×10⁻⁷ m², so the weight is 200×10⁶ × 1.96×10⁻⁷ ≈ 39 N. The lift is 100 mm × 0.040 = 4.0 mm, and the work is 39 × 4.0×10⁻³ ≈ 0.16 J. This equals σε = 8 MJ/m³ per unit volume times the volume of the wire. About 0.63 J uses the diameter as the radius, making the area four times too large. About 0.079 J includes a factor of 1/2 as for the elastic energy of a spring, but the weight's force is constant throughout the contraction, so there is no 1/2. Shape memory alloys deliver a large work per unit volume and can serve as small, light actuators, but heating and cooling take time, so they are poor at fast motion.

functional-alloys-020.question: In the PCT curves of hydrogen storage alloys, the plateau pressure for absorbing hydrogen is higher than that for desorbing it, even at the same temperature (hysteresis). What is the main reason?
choices: Only during absorption must hydrogen molecules dissociate into atoms at the surface, whereas during desorption the hydrogen can leave as atoms
The hydride expands the lattice greatly, so extra work for misfit strain and plastic deformation shifts the absorption and desorption equilibria apart
The temperature falls during the measurement, so according to the van 't Hoff equation the plateau pressure for desorption appears lower
functional-alloys-020.explanation: When a hydrogen storage alloy becomes a hydride, its lattice expands greatly; for LaNi₅ the volume increases by about 25%. When the hydride forms within the solid-solution phase, and conversely when it reverts to the solid solution, extra energy is needed for the elastic strain and plastic deformation caused by the volume difference between the two phases, so absorption needs a higher pressure and desorption a lower one, and the two plateau pressures separate. Repeated expansion and contraction also cracks the particles into fine powder (decrepitation). During desorption, hydrogen atoms recombine into molecules at the surface before leaving, so saying that dissociation is needed only for absorption is wrong. Hysteresis appears even in measurements at constant temperature.

functional-alloys-021.question: A superelastic Ti-Ni wire is pulled. On loading, a transformation strain of 6.0% develops at a nearly constant stress of 500 MPa, and on unloading it recovers at a nearly constant 200 MPa. Ignoring the elastic parts and treating the stress–strain curve as this rectangular loop, which is closest to the energy per unit volume lost as heat in one loading–unloading cycle?
choices: About 30 MJ/m³
About 18 MJ/m³
About 12 MJ/m³
functional-alloys-021.explanation: The work done on loading is 500 MPa × 0.060 = 30 MJ/m³ and the work returned on unloading is 200 MPa × 0.060 = 12 MJ/m³, so the difference, (500 − 200) × 0.060 = 18 MJ/m³ (18 J/cm³), is the area of the loop and is turned into heat in every cycle. About 30 MJ/m³ counts only the loading work, and about 12 MJ/m³ mistakes the returned energy for the lost energy. The transformation stresses differ on loading and unloading because moving the transformation interfaces meets a friction-like resistance, and the large loop area has been studied for use in vibration-damping members. Conversely, when the wire is used as a spring, the returning force is smaller by the amount that is lost.

functional-alloys-022.question: A metal-hydride tank absorbs 1.0 kg of hydrogen. If the enthalpy of hydride formation is ΔH = −30 kJ/mol H₂, which is closest to the heat that must be removed from the tank during absorption? Take the molar mass of H₂ as 2.016 g/mol.
choices: About 15 MJ
About 30 MJ
About 7.4 MJ
functional-alloys-022.explanation: 1.0 kg of hydrogen is 1000/2.016 ≈ 496 mol of H₂, so the heat released is 496 × 30 kJ ≈ 1.49×10⁴ kJ, about 15 MJ. If this heat is not removed, the alloy warms up, the plateau pressure rises according to the van 't Hoff equation, and absorption stalls. During release the same amount of heat must be supplied instead. About 30 MJ counts moles of H atoms (about 992 mol), and about 7.4 MJ halves ΔH to a value per mole of H atoms and then multiplies it by the moles of H₂. Fifteen megajoules is a little over a tenth of the lower heating value of 1 kg of hydrogen (about 120 MJ), so the heat exchange of the tank is an important part of its design.

functional-alloys-023.question: When a superelastic Ti-Ni wire is loaded and unloaded to the same strain dozens of times, its stress–strain curve gradually changes. Which correctly describes the change and its cause?
choices: The transformation stress rises and the loop keeps widening, because cycling work-hardens the parent phase so that transformation needs a larger force
The curve does not change at all until fracture, because the transformation only shifts atoms slightly, creates no dislocations and fully restores the structure
The transformation stress falls and unrecovered strain slowly builds up, because the moving interfaces leave dislocations whose internal stress aids transformation
functional-alloys-023.explanation: With repeated stress-induced martensitic transformation, each back-and-forth motion of the parent–martensite interfaces leaves a few dislocations around them, and some martensite stays untransformed. The internal stress around the dislocations acts in the direction that assists transformation, so the stress at which transformation starts falls, unrecovered (residual) strain accumulates and the loop area shrinks. These changes are largest in the first cycles and usually level off after some tens to about a hundred cycles, so the material is sometimes cycled before use to stabilize its behavior. The claim that the transformation stress keeps rising has the direction of change reversed. The claim that the transformation creates no dislocations does not fit the observed change in behavior with cycling.

functional-alloys-024.question: In LaNi₅₋ₓAlₓ, where part of the Ni in LaNi₅ is replaced by Al, the plateau pressure at a given temperature changes. Which correctly gives the direction of the change and its reason? Assume that Al atoms are larger than Ni atoms.
choices: It rises, because in the expanded lattice hydrogen sits farther from the metal atoms, bonds more weakly and the hydride becomes less stable
It falls, because the lattice expands, the interstices for hydrogen become larger and the hydride becomes more stable
It does not change, because Al absorbs no hydrogen; only the capacity falls, and the plateau pressure is set by the La content alone
functional-alloys-024.explanation: In AB₅ alloys, substitutions that enlarge the unit-cell volume widen the interstitial sites that hydrogen occupies, stabilize the hydride and tend to lower the plateau pressure (the logarithm of the plateau pressure is known to vary almost linearly with the cell volume). Replacing Ni with larger Al or Mn lowers the plateau pressure, whereas replacing La with smaller Ce and similar elements (as in MmNi₅ made with mischmetal) raises it. Substitutions like these are used to tune the plateau pressure to a convenient value at the operating temperature. Al substitution does reduce the capacity somewhat, but the plateau pressure does not stay the same.

functional-alloys-025.question: You want a Ti-Ni wire to memorize a new shape, such as a coil spring. Which is the usual method?
choices: Fix the wire in the desired shape with a fixture, heat-treat it in that shape at around 500 °C and then cool it
Bend the wire into the desired shape below Mf, hold it there for a while and then release the load
Heat the wire close to its melting point to melt it, pour it into a mold of the desired shape and quench it
functional-alloys-025.explanation: The shape a shape memory alloy returns to is the shape it has in the parent phase. When a cold-worked Ti-Ni wire is constrained in the desired shape with a fixture and heat-treated at around 500 °C, the dislocations stored by working rearrange (and in Ni-rich alloys precipitation also occurs), so that shape becomes the strain-free shape of the parent phase. This is called shape setting, and the temperature and time also shift the transformation temperatures. Bending below Mf only reorients the martensite variants, so the wire returns to its old shape on heating and no new shape is memorized. Melting and casting gives a coarse cast structure and is not a way to set the shape of a thin wire or spring.
